Tulsi Health: Choosing the Number

Bengaluru, February 2026. A product head has nine days to name the one number her team will be held to for the next year — and the easiest number available is the one she trusts least.

1. Nine days

On the evening of Monday, 9 February 2026, Aditi Rane stayed back after the Bengaluru office had emptied, in the second-floor conference room that Tulsi Health's staff called the Fishbowl. On the whiteboard behind her, still unerased from the morning's stand-up, was a single line in her chief executive's handwriting: One number for the board, one for the team. 18 Feb.

Aditi had been Tulsi Health's head of product for fourteen months. The company's board was meeting on Wednesday, 18 February, to approve the annual plan for Tulsi Care Plus, the ₹6,000-a-year chronic-care subscription that had grown from nothing to 74,000 paying members in twenty-two months. The plan asked investors for ₹92 crore. The chief executive, Sanjay Kabra, had told her plainly that the plan would not be approved without a credible measure of whether the product was working, and that "downloads and daily actives will not survive the first question from the Elevar partner."

The difficulty was not a shortage of numbers. Tulsi's event pipeline logged 284 distinct events. The difficulty was that the number Aditi most trusted — whether a member's diabetes was actually better controlled — arrived once every six months, and the numbers that arrived daily had stopped meaning anything she could defend.

2. Company background

Tulsi Health was founded in 2021 in Bengaluru by Sanjay Kabra, a former Practo product leader, and Dr Meenal Joshi, an endocrinologist from Pune. It sold a subscription for people managing Type 2 diabetes: a Bluetooth glucometer posted to the member's home, an app that logged readings and meals, a monthly video consultation with a physician, and unlimited chat access to a diabetes coach. The price was ₹6,000 a year, collected through Razorpay, with roughly 71 per cent of payments arriving over UPI.

The market around it was crowded and getting more so. Tata 1mg and Apollo 24|7 bundled diagnostics and pharmacy; HealthifyMe had built a large coaching business on weight; Practo owned the consultation habit. Tulsi's differentiation was narrow and clinical: it claimed, and its own data suggested, that members who stayed engaged for six months reduced their HbA1c — the standard three-month average blood-sugar measure — by an average of 0.8 percentage points. That claim was the entire investment thesis. It was also why Tulsi had, in 2025, begun the work of connecting to the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission's health records framework, and why its consent flows had been rebuilt twice under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, which constrained how long identifiable behavioural data could be retained and for what stated purpose.

Two revenue lines had grown alongside the consumer subscription. An employer channel, sold in the United States by Michael D'Souza out of New Jersey to Indian-origin employee populations, contributed ₹8 crore. And a single large corporate wellness contract with a facilities-management group in Dubai, worth ₹4.6 crore a year, was up for renewal in July 2026.

3. The situation

The metric Tulsi had reported to its board for six quarters was DAU/MAU — daily active members divided by monthly active members — supplemented by "log streak" length. Both had been chosen in 2022 when the product was an app with a glucometer and nothing else, and both had been rising: DAU/MAU from 0.21 to 0.34 over eighteen months, average streak from 4.1 days to 9.6.

In December 2025, Farhan Qureshi, Tulsi's data scientist in Toronto, had sent Aditi a note at 6.40 a.m. India time that unsettled the whole plan. He had pulled the 2024 joining cohorts through to their twelve-month renewal decision and found that DAU/MAU had almost no relationship to renewal within the engaged population, and that streak length had a slightly negative relationship above about fifteen days. His hypothesis was uncomfortable: the streak nudges Lena Hoffmann's design team had shipped in Berlin in early 2024 had successfully taught members to open the app and log a reading every morning, and the members who complied most diligently were disproportionately the ones who were anxious about their condition — and who, when their numbers did not improve, cancelled.

Meanwhile Grace Tan, running customer success from Singapore, had a different observation from the Dubai contract. The client's HR head did not care about app opens at all. He cared whether his 1,400 enrolled workers were showing up for their annual medical check with better readings, and whether the coaches were reachable during the shifts his workers actually worked.

Aditi's view, formed over January, was that Tulsi had never asked what its members were trying to achieve and worked forward from there. It had asked what the app could count. Exhibits 1 to 3 were what she assembled to make that case, and to choose differently.

4. The people

Sanjay Kabra, chief executive, Bengaluru. Wants a number the board will accept without a tutorial, and wants it to be comparable to what HealthifyMe and Apollo 24|7 quote publicly. Has said twice that "we cannot go to the board and say our old metric was wrong."

Dr Meenal Joshi, co-founder and clinical head, Pune. Wants the company held to HbA1c improvement and nothing else. Regards engagement metrics as "a marketing department measuring its own applause," and has threatened, mildly, to write a dissenting note to the board.

Farhan Qureshi, data scientist, Toronto. Wants the metric chosen from the cohort evidence rather than negotiated in a room. Has flagged that whatever is chosen, the DPDP consent language limits behavioural data retention to eighteen months for identifiable members, which caps how long any correlation can be re-validated.

Lena Hoffmann, design lead, Berlin. Built the streak system and is not defensive about it, but wants any new metric to be something design can actually move in a quarter. Has pointed out that the coach chat is the only surface members describe warmly in research, and that it is not instrumented at all beyond message counts.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Candidate metrics against twelve-month renewal, 2024 joining cohorts (n = 31,600)

Taken together the three exhibits say something narrower than "our metrics are wrong." Exhibit 3 establishes that eighteen months of successful engagement growth moved renewal by less than the noise in the series. Exhibit 1 explains why: the metrics Tulsi had been improving were the ones with the least discriminating power, and the streak metric that design had worked hardest on separated members in the wrong direction. Exhibit 2 is the interesting one, because it is not drawn from the event log at all. Aditi built it by writing down what a member had told her in a research call in Chennai — "I want my numbers to be normal at my next check-up and I want to stop worrying about every meal" — and then asking what a member doing that visibly does: measures, sees readings in band, and has someone answer when they do not. The three components in Exhibit 2 are those actions. The 78 per cent against 29 per cent spread in Exhibit 1 is the first evidence that the derivation was sound. It is also, at 13 per cent of members, a number that would look poor next to anything Tulsi had previously reported.

6. The options

Option A — Keep DAU/MAU for the board and set a streak target for the team. The number is instrumented, has six quarters of history, needs no new engineering, and is comparable to what competitors quote. Sanjay would not have to explain a reversal. The cost is that Exhibits 1 and 3 say the number does not track the thing the investment thesis rests on, and that a streak target would push Lena's team towards more notifications, which Farhan's analysis suggests correlates with cancellation among the most anxious members. If the board approves ₹92 crore against this number, Tulsi will spend a year optimising it.

Option B — Adopt HbA1c improvement as the single metric, as Dr Joshi wants. It is the outcome the company actually sells and the one the Dubai client's HR head cares about. It is unimpeachable in a board meeting. The cost is cadence and coverage: HbA1c arrives from a lab test roughly every six months, only 44 per cent of members submit one at all, and submission is itself correlated with doing well. A team of twenty-six engineers cannot steer on two observations a year, and the metric would tell Aditi nothing before the Dubai renewal in July.

Option C — Report HbA1c improvement to the board as the outcome, and adopt "in-range weeks" as the team's weekly metric. This requires spending ₹35 lakh and six weeks of two Pune engineers to instrument the coach-reply event properly, delaying two roadmap items; accepting a baseline of 13 per cent that looks weak; and asking the board to hold Tulsi to a number none of its competitors quote. In exchange Aditi gets a leading indicator with a 49-point renewal spread, derived from a member goal rather than an event log, that design and clinical can both act on within a quarter.

7. Questions for discussion

1. What exactly was wrong with the way Tulsi chose DAU/MAU and log streaks in 2022, given that both were accurate and both improved?

2. Work through Exhibit 2. Which of the three components of "in-range weeks" is doing most of the discriminating work in Exhibit 1, and what would you need to know to find out?

3. Dr Joshi and Sanjay Kabra are both right about something. What is each of them right about, and what would a metric system that honoured both look like?

4. What should Aditi take to the board on 18 February, and what is the strongest objection to her choice that she should answer before it is raised?

8. A note for the learner

This case is a worked instance of the GAME framework: Goals, Actions, Metrics, Evaluate. The framework's claim is not that some metrics are better than others in the abstract, but that the direction of derivation determines whether a metric can be trusted. Tulsi derived backwards — from the event log to a chart to a goal written above the chart — and got numbers that were accurate, improvable and irrelevant. Aditi's Exhibit 2 was derived forwards: a member goal stated in the member's words, then the observable actions of a member achieving it, then a metric with a defined numerator, denominator and window, and only then a target.

A well-reasoned answer will separate two questions that the room keeps conflating. The first is what Tulsi should report — a question about credibility with a board, where the slow, unimpeachable outcome metric belongs. The second is what Tulsi's team should steer on weekly — a question about cadence and controllability, where a derived leading indicator belongs. Dr Joshi and Sanjay Kabra are each answering only one of these and treating it as the whole question. A strong answer will also notice that Exhibit 1's headline spread is correlational: members who achieve in-range weeks may simply be the members who were going to do well anyway, so the honest next step is an experiment on prompting the behaviour, not a target set as though the full 49 points will transfer.

One defensible path is Option C with three conditions attached. First, report HbA1c improvement plus renewal to the board as the outcomes, and present "in-range weeks" explicitly as the input metric the product team will own — which answers Sanjay's objection, because nothing previously reported is retracted; a new, more demanding layer is added beneath it. Second, fund the ₹35 lakh instrumentation now and accept the roadmap delay, because Exhibit 2's coach-reply component is currently a manual estimate and a metric that cannot be computed will quietly decay into whatever the warehouse can serve. Third, complete step E properly: Aditi owns the number, it is reviewed every Monday, the target for the quarter is 13 to 22 per cent, and a stated decision is written in advance — if in-range weeks stays below 16 per cent by the end of April, Tulsi stops adding content and rebuilds coach responsiveness during the shift hours Grace Tan's Dubai members actually work. That last clause, uncomfortable and specific, is what distinguishes a chosen metric from a displayed one.

The GAME Framework: Deriving Metrics from Goals

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Ananya Deshpande, head of product at Charkha Fitness in Pune, opened the board deck two days before her Series B data room closed and found the same slide that had troubled her for a month. Daily active users were up 22% quarter on quarter. Ninety-day retention was flat at 31%. Revenue per user had not moved. Her CEO's note in the margin read: "Investors will ask what our north star is. What do we say?" Charkha had eleven dashboards, forty-three tracked events, and no single number anyone could defend in a room. Ananya had two days to decide not which number looked best, but which number meant something — and to do that she had to stop looking at what the analytics stack already counted and start from what her users were actually trying to accomplish.

Figure 1. The GAME sequence: a metric is only as good as the goal and action it was derived from.

The idea

GAME is a disciplined sequence for building metrics: state the user's Goal in the user's own language, name the observable Actions a user takes when making progress on that goal, convert those actions into countable Metrics, and then Evaluate each metric by giving it a target, an owner, a review cadence, and the decision it is meant to inform. It was not invented by a single named researcher the way the balanced scorecard or net promoter score were; it crystallized through the 2010s inside growth and analytics teams at consumer internet companies as a teaching mnemonic, and it now appears, in close variants, in the instrumentation modules of most digital-product-management courses, including those at Wharton, Haas, and Darden. It exists to solve one specific and recurring failure: teams build dashboards out of whatever the event-logging pipeline already captures — app opens, page views, button taps — and then mistake a full dashboard for a measured business. GAME reverses the order of operations. The single sentence Ananya could repeat in the boardroom without sounding glib is this: we don't measure what we can count, we count what proves the user got what they came for.

How it actually works

The first step, Goals, is harder than it looks because it must be written from the user's vantage point, not the company's. "Increase 90-day retention" is a company goal; it belongs at the Evaluate stage, not here. The user's goal at Charkha Fitness might be "build an exercise habit I can actually keep up" — a sentence a real member would say, which a product manager typically only arrives at through interviews, support-ticket reading, or onboarding-survey text, not through the event schema. Practitioners routinely skip this step's most implicit requirement: writing the goal down in a full sentence and testing whether a real user would recognize it as their own, rather than paraphrasing a feature list.

The second step, Actions, asks what a user does — observably, in the product — when they are succeeding at that goal, as distinct from everything they do while merely present in the app. Scheduling a workout, completing it, and returning three days later after a planned rest day are actions tied to habit formation; opening the app and scrolling the feed is not, however frequently it happens, because it carries no information about progress toward the stated goal. This is the step where teams most often quietly cheat, substituting "things we already log" for "things that indicate the goal," which is precisely the failure GAME was built to catch.

The third step, Metrics, turns each action into something countable, and forces a choice practitioners often leave implicit: whether the count should be a raw magnitude (workouts completed per user per week) or a ratio (share of scheduled workouts actually completed), and whether it should measure the goal directly or stand in for it as a proxy, because the goal itself — a sustained habit, a feeling of health — is often not directly observable in any single event. The fourth step, Evaluate, is where most teams stop too early: a metric without a numeric target, a named owner, a stated review cadence, and an explicit decision it will trigger is not yet a managed metric, only a number somebody happened to notice.

A worked example

Ananya ran twelve short user interviews over one evening and found two distinct goal clusters among Charkha's roughly 62,000 monthly active members: a "habit builder" cohort (about 70% of new signups) whose stated goal was sustainable, ongoing fitness, and an "event-driven" cohort (about 30%) training for a specific date — a wedding, a half-marathon — after which usage was expected to taper. She built the GAME chain for the larger cohort first.

StepCharkha Fitness — habit-builder cohort
Goal"I want exercise to become something I just do, without having to talk myself into it every time."
ActionsSchedules a workout in advance; completes a scheduled workout; returns to train within 48 hours of a rest day; logs a completed session without prompting.
MetricsWorkouts completed per active user per week (magnitude); 7-day scheduled-to-completed ratio (ratio); Day-28 habit retention: % of Week-4 cohort with ≥3 sessions/week.
EvaluateTarget 45% for Day-28 habit retention; owner: growth PM; reviewed weekly; if it falls below 40% for two consecutive weeks, paid acquisition spend is paused pending a product review.

The arithmetic behind the primary metric: of 10,000 new habit-builder signups in a monthly cohort, 6,400 completed a first workout in week one (64%), 3,900 were still training by week four, and of those, 1,833 trained three or more sessions in that fourth week — a Day-28 habit retention rate of 18.3% (1,833 ÷ 10,000), well under the 45% target, which is precisely the number Ananya could not have produced from "DAU up 22%."

Running the same chain for the event-driven cohort changes the answer, not just the number but the shape of the metric itself. Their goal is "I want to be ready by a fixed date," so the correct action is not sustained weekly training but completion of a structured program by its deadline, and the correct metric is program-completion rate within the target window, not Day-28 habit retention — applying the habit metric to this cohort would show them "churning" when they were in fact succeeding and leaving on schedule. Of 4,300 event-driven signups, 2,795 (65%) completed their chosen program before its target date, a healthy result that the original single retention curve had been quietly averaging down.

The nuances

Goals belong to the user, not the P&L

The most common blur is writing a company objective — "grow revenue," "reduce churn" — into the Goal slot. Those are legitimate targets for the Evaluate stage, where the business decides what it wants, but if they sit in the Goal slot the whole chain downstream measures the company's convenience, not the user's success, and metrics built on it will optimize behavior the user never asked for.

An action must be evidence of progress, not just presence

An event is only a GAME action if its absence would mean the user is not making progress. "App opened" almost never qualifies on its own; "workout completed" does. Teams confuse frequency of an event with relevance of an event constantly, because frequency is easier to query.

Direct metrics versus proxy metrics

Some goals are directly observable — "complete this workout" can be logged exactly. Others, like "feel confident in my body" or "trust this brand," cannot be logged at all, so the metric is necessarily a proxy (a survey score, a referral rate) standing in for something unmeasured. GAME does not remove the proxy problem; it forces the team to notice which kind of metric it built and to say so out loud.

Magnitude metrics versus ratio metrics

A count (workouts per week) and a rate (share of scheduled sessions completed) answer different questions and can move in opposite directions in the same period — completions can rise even as the completion rate falls, if scheduling volume rises faster. A GAME chain that reports only one of the two is only half informative.

One goal can spawn several defensible metrics

Multiplicity is not a flaw in the method; a single goal legitimately produces a small family of metrics at different steps of the journey. The discipline GAME adds is insisting the team then choose one as primary for decision-making, rather than reporting all of them and letting nobody be accountable for any.

GAME does not tell you what number is good enough

The framework produces the right metric; it does not produce the right target. Forty-five percent Day-28 habit retention was a judgment Ananya made from competitor benchmarking and her own cohort history, not something GAME derived. Teams that expect the method to hand them a threshold are asking it to do a job it was never built for.

Once a target exists, Goodhart's risk begins

The moment a metric acquires a target and an owner, people will find the cheapest way to move it, which is not always the way that serves the original goal — nudging users to log workouts they didn't do, for instance, would lift the metric while destroying the thing it was meant to represent. GAME reduces this risk by keeping the goal sentence visible next to the metric, but it cannot eliminate it.

GAME degrades without real user research behind Goals

If the Goal step is filled in from a product manager's assumption rather than from actual interviews, support transcripts, or survey text, the entire chain still looks methodologically correct while measuring a fiction. The framework is only as honest as the research that feeds its first letter.

Consumer, B2B, and marketplace — and early versus late stage

In a consumer product like Charkha, one user typically holds one goal, actions are frequent, and metrics can be evaluated weekly with statistically meaningful cohorts within days. At a B2B company such as Devanshi Cloud, a workflow-automation platform sold to finance teams, the goal splits across two people — the admin who bought the software wants faster month-end close, while the analyst who uses it daily wants fewer manual reconciliations — and GAME has to be run twice, once per goal-holder, because a single metric chain flattens two different definitions of success into one number that satisfies neither. Actions are also sparser and slower: an admin's meaningful action might occur monthly, at close, so the Evaluate cadence has to move from weekly to monthly or quarterly, tied to the renewal cycle rather than the sprint cycle.

In a marketplace such as Anaadi Marketplace, connecting home-repair contractors with households, the Goal step must be written twice again, for buyer and for seller, and the Metrics step has to guard against optimizing one side at the other's expense — a metric that raises booking completion for households by flooding contractors with unpaid leads will look excellent on one side of the GAME chain and be quietly destroying the other. Early-stage teams, with only a few hundred users, usually cannot yet run statistically stable ratio metrics and lean more heavily on qualitative confirmation of the Goal step itself; late-stage teams, with goals well validated over years, shift their effort toward guarding the Evaluate step against Goodhart's law, since a large organization has far more people with an incentive to move a metric the cheap way.

Common mistakes

Mistake 1 — starting from Metrics, not Goals. Symptom: a dashboard full of session counts, screen views, and taps that nobody can connect to a user outcome. Underlying error: building metrics from whatever the logging pipeline already emits, because that is easier than interviewing users. Cheapest diagnostic: for every tile on the dashboard, ask "which sentence, in a user's own words, does this number represent?" — a tile with no answer is a candidate for deletion.

Mistake 2 — treating any logged event as an Action. Symptom: "app opened" or "notification tapped" reported as a core product metric. Underlying error: confusing instrumentation convenience with behavioral evidence. Cheapest diagnostic: ask whether the event could occur at high volume while the user's stated goal goes completely unmet — if yes, it is not a GAME action.

Mistake 3 — stopping at Metrics and skipping Evaluate. Symptom: a metric gets a slide in one all-hands, is admired, and is never mentioned again because no one owns it. Underlying error: treating measurement as a reporting exercise rather than a decision mechanism. Cheapest diagnostic: ask "what specific action does the team take differently if this number moves ten percent next month?" — no answer means no owner and no real metric.

Mistake 4 — one metric across cohorts with different goals. Symptom: an aggregate curve that looks flat or mediocre even though two underlying groups are each doing exactly what they should. Underlying error: assuming all users share one goal because they share one product. Cheapest diagnostic: segment the metric by the inferred goal cluster before concluding anything is wrong.

What good looks like

Picture the same decision at Charkha Fitness handled well: before building anything, Ananya's team interviews members, discovers the two goal clusters, writes each goal as a full sentence, and builds two separate GAME chains rather than forcing one metric to serve both. Day-28 habit retention becomes the primary number for 70% of the base; program-completion-by-deadline becomes the primary number for the other 30%. Each has a named owner, a stated target grounded in prior cohorts and competitor data, a review cadence matched to how fast the underlying behavior actually changes, and an explicit trigger — pause acquisition spend, escalate to a product review — tied to it moving the wrong way. When the board asks for the north star, the team does not produce one flattering number; it produces a short, defensible chain from a sentence a real member said in an interview to the number on the slide, and everyone in the room can see exactly how one led to the other.

Closing

Ananya presented both chains to Charkha's board two days later: Day-28 habit retention at 18.3%, well short of the 45% target, with program completion at 65% for the event-driven cohort held up as evidence the product itself worked when the goal matched the metric. Rather than defend a single flattering aggregate, she recommended splitting the onboarding flow by inferred goal within thirty days and reviewing habit retention weekly, owned by growth, with acquisition spend paused if it stayed under 40% for two straight weeks. The board did not get a comforting number; they got a legible one, and a plan tied to it. From here, the natural next things to learn are the distinction between direct and proxy metrics and between magnitude and ratio metrics, both of which GAME surfaces but does not resolve on its own, and the acquisition, retention, and monetization action families that most consumer GAME chains eventually converge on. Two questions worth sitting with: when you last built a dashboard, did you write the user's goal as a full sentence first, or did you start from the columns already sitting in your database? And for the metric you currently trust the most, who owns it, how often is it reviewed, and what decision actually changes when it moves?

Nivasa Services: The Number Before the Board

Bengaluru, the night of Sunday 8 March 2026. A chief product officer has one page to write by nine the next morning, four numbers that cannot all be true, and a term sheet that assumes she already knows the answer.

1. The night before

Rhea Bhattacharya had been at the dining table in her flat off Sarjapur Road since half past eight, and the Holi crackers from the compound below had stopped about an hour ago. In front of her were four printouts, each with a different number on it, each produced by a colleague she trusted, and each answering a slightly different question from the one she had asked.

At nine the next morning the board pre-read for Nivasa Services was due with the company secretary. Section 3 of that pre-read was a single page titled "Our metric system for FY27," and Kartik Soni, the founder and chief executive, had asked for exactly one number at the top of it. Elevar Growth Partners, leading the proposed ₹640 crore Series E, had made the request more pointed in a note the previous Tuesday: "We would like to understand which single operating metric the management team is running the business on, and to see twenty-four months of it."

Rhea had drafted the page three times. The first draft had used the number her growth team had reported for four years. The second had used the number her data platform team believed was the only defensible one. The third had used neither, and had felt, when she read it back at eleven, like a confession rather than a plan.

2. Company history, and the decision that still binds

Nivasa Services had been founded in 2019 in Bengaluru by Kartik Soni and two classmates from NIT Trichy, as a marketplace for home services: deep cleaning, appliance repair, plumbing, pest control, and salon-at-home treatments. In its first two years it looked like dozens of other listings businesses. Customers posted a requirement, independent professionals quoted, and Nivasa took a 12 per cent commission on whatever they agreed. The catalogue was wide, the pricing was chaotic, and the completion rate was 61 per cent.

In August 2022 the founders made the decision that defined everything since. They killed the quoting model and moved to what the industry calls managed supply: Nivasa set the price, Nivasa assigned the professional, Nivasa trained and certified them, and Nivasa's app became the only legitimate channel through which a job could be booked, priced and paid. Completion rose to 94 per cent within nine months. Average order value rose from ₹640 to ₹1,180. The company raised a Series D of ₹310 crore in early 2023 on the strength of those numbers, and by February 2026 it operated in nine cities with roughly 38,000 active professionals and an annualised gross merchandise value of about ₹1,140 crore.

The move to managed supply also rebuilt the data model, and this is the constraint that still binds. To make central assignment work, Devesh Iyer's platform team had made the job the atomic unit of the warehouse: every event in the system hung off a job identifier. It was a clean schema and it served operations beautifully. But it meant that Nivasa's customer-side analytics had no stable notion of a household, only of a billing account; that a professional's identity appeared on the supply side of the warehouse and not in the customer's event stream at all; and that anything happening inside the customer's home — which was, after all, the service — was represented by a single terminal field, job_status = completed, plus a star rating. Four years of instrumentation had been layered on top of that schema. Re-basing it on a household-and-relationship model had been quoted, in January 2026, at ₹18 crore and eleven months.

3. The industry around it

By 2026 the Indian home-services market was no longer a land grab. Urban Company had established the category and the consumer expectation of a fixed price and a uniformed professional. Amazon and Flipkart had both run services experiments and pulled back to narrow slices. Reliance Retail had begun bundling appliance installation and repair with its own electronics sales, which mattered because appliance repair was Nivasa's highest-margin category. Local aggregators in Pune, Kochi and Lucknow competed on price with a fraction of Nivasa's cost base. And the services network on ONDC had begun, slowly and unevenly, to let a customer in Jaipur book a plumber through a payments app they already had, which threatened to turn discovery into a commodity exactly where Nivasa had spent four years building brand.

Regulation had moved too, and in a direction that made partner economics a board-level matter rather than an operations one. Rajasthan's platform-based gig workers legislation of 2023 and the Karnataka ordinance that followed established registration, welfare-fee and transparency obligations towards platform workers; the welfare cess in Karnataka, at the rate Nivasa's finance team was modelling, would cost roughly ₹14 crore a year on current volumes in that state alone. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act constrained what Nivasa could retain and infer about customers and professionals, and had already forced the removal of a feature that scored professionals partly on their phone's location history between jobs. GST classification disputes on composite service-plus-materials bookings had been running for two years.

Nivasa's exposure was not only Indian. Bradley Okafor, hired in New Jersey in 2024, had sold a white-label version of the booking and dispatch stack to two American property-management groups, contributing ₹21 crore. Wei Ling Chan, running enterprise customer success out of Singapore, managed the single largest contract on the books: Marasi Estates, a Dubai property group that had bought managed home services for 6,000 serviced apartments at ₹47 crore a year, with a renewal review in September 2026 and a service-level annexe that specified reporting Nivasa's warehouse could not currently produce without manual reconciliation.

4. The situation in detail

Nivasa's reported operating metric since 2022 had been monthly transacting customers, or MTC: billing accounts with at least one completed job in the calendar month. In February 2026 it stood at 1.42 million, up from 0.96 million two years earlier. Ira Menon's growth organisation in Mumbai was measured on it, planned against it, and had hit it in nineteen of the last twenty-four months.

The trouble began in June 2025, with the launch of Nivasa Plus at ₹1,499 a year — a membership offering priority slots, a 10 per cent discount and a service guarantee. It had sold 310,000 memberships by February 2026, and Ira's team celebrated it as the year's best growth product. In September, Anouk Weber's design research team in Berlin ran thirty-two home visits across Bengaluru, Pune and Lucknow, and came back with a finding nobody had asked for: Plus members described the product in terms that had nothing to do with slots or discounts. What they said, repeatedly, was some version of "I want one person who knows my house." Fourteen of the thirty-two had, at some point, taken a professional's phone number and booked directly off-platform for small jobs, while keeping the membership for the guarantee on large ones.

Anouk's finding sat unexamined for two months, because nothing in the warehouse could test it. Then, in November 2025, Nivasa shipped AI auto-scheduling: a model that proposed a slot and a professional to the customer at booking, with the proposal pre-selected. Acceptance rate in the first quarter was 88 per cent, which Ira's dashboard reported as strong product-market fit for the feature. In January 2026, Devesh Iyer's team ran a late audit and found that the 88 per cent included every booking in which the customer simply proceeded without changing the default — and that among Plus members who had previously had a repeat professional, the model assigned that same professional 23 per cent of the time, because its objective function was fill-rate and travel time, not continuity.

Then the two contradictions arrived within a fortnight of each other. On 2 February, Devesh's team delivered a cohort analysis showing that jobs per customer per year had fallen from 3.4 for the 2023 cohort to 2.6 for the 2025 cohort, and that twelve-month repeat had fallen from 58 to 49 per cent — while MTC grew, because acquisition was growing faster than repeat was falling. On 11 February, Ira's team delivered its quarterly brand-and-intent study, conducted by a Gurugram agency, reporting that stated repurchase intent among Nivasa customers had risen from 71 to 79 per cent and satisfaction from 4.1 to 4.4. Both studies were competently done. They pointed opposite ways.

Meanwhile Farida Sheikh, who ran supply operations from Pune, had her own deteriorating series. Professional ninety-day retention had fallen from 74 per cent for the 2024 joining cohorts to 61 per cent for 2025, and earnings per active hour, after the platform fee and the materials pass-through, had drifted from ₹214 to ₹198. Farida's reading was that auto-scheduling had increased the number of unfamiliar first visits, which took longer, paid the same, and generated more disputes. She had said so in the December operations review. The minutes recorded it as "supply sentiment to be monitored."

GAME at Depth: Why the Action Step Carries the Weight

Two rooms, one unresolved question

On 4 February 2026, in a glass room above Bengaluru's Bellandur lake, Rukmini Gokhale, vice-president of product at Tulja Fresh, was looking at two competing metric chains on the same whiteboard. Tulja Fresh ran thirty-minute grocery delivery across seven cities: 1.4 million monthly buyers, ₹ 310 crore of annualised gross order value, a contribution margin still eleven rupees short of breakeven per order. Her growth team wanted the activation metric to be second order within ten days; her data-science lead wanted saved a repeat basket in the first fortnight, which predicted ninety-day survival far more sharply. Both were honest readings of the same cohort table. Only one could carry a target, an owner and a quarterly bonus, and the operating plan locked in eight days.

Five weeks later, on 11 March, Devdatta Rane, chief product officer at Sankalan Health Cloud in Hyderabad, faced the same problem with the opposite data endowment. Sankalan sold clinical-documentation software to hospital chains: 140 accounts, ₹ 62 crore of ARR, an average contract of ₹ 44 lakh, renewals decided once a year by committee. Two accounts had churned in January, both with healthy login numbers until the week they left. Devdatta needed a leading indicator of renewal, had 140 data points in total — fewer observations than Rukmini generated in four seconds — and a board that wanted the number by the April review.

The GAME sequence — Goals, Actions, Metrics, Evaluate — is usually taught as a way of escaping dashboards built from whatever the event pipeline happens to emit. That framing is correct and insufficient. The argument of this page is narrower: almost everything that goes wrong with GAME goes wrong at the Action step, because that is the only step where a team makes a falsifiable claim about the world — that a particular observable behaviour is evidence of progress toward a goal. Goals are hard to write but cheap to revise; metrics and evaluation are largely bookkeeping once the Action is right. The Action is where a chain is either load-bearing or decorative, and it is the step most teams fill in by convenience.

The idea, its ancestry, and who disagrees

A GAME chain is a four-part commitment: a Goal written as a sentence in the user's own language; a set of Actions, observable in the product, whose occurrence is evidence of progress toward that goal; Metrics counting those actions in a defined population over a defined window; and an Evaluate step attaching to each metric a target, an owner, a cadence and the decision the number informs.

The lineage explains the disagreements. The direct ancestor is Goal-Question-Metric, formulated by Victor Basili and colleagues at the University of Maryland in the 1980s for software-engineering measurement: state a goal, derive the questions that would tell you whether it is met, then derive metrics that answer them. Alongside it sit Kaplan and Norton's balanced scorecard (1992); Google's HEART framework (Rodden, Hutchinson and Fu, 2010), which paired user-centred metric categories with an explicit goals-signals-metrics derivation; and the growth-analytics practice of the 2010s, popularised through Croll and Yoskovitz's Lean Analytics and Sean Ellis's activation work, which supplied the vocabulary of activation events and north stars. GAME crystallised out of that confluence in digital-product-management curricula at Wharton, Haas and Darden.

The substantive difference is the middle letter. GQM interposes a Question — an analyst's epistemic need — and so admits metrics no user behaviour produces, such as a survey score or an expert audit. GAME interposes an Action, a user's behaviour, and is thus a behaviourist restriction on GQM: in a digital product the only evidence obtainable continuously, at population scale and without asking, is behaviour, and a measurement programme built on anything else will not survive contact with a weekly operating rhythm.

Figure 1. GQM and GAME differ at the middle term. Substituting Action for Question buys continuous, population-scale measurement and pays for it by excluding goals no behaviour reveals.

Four schools disagree about what follows. The behaviourist school signs that no metric belongs on an operating dashboard unless a logged user behaviour produces it; it will not sign that attitudinal measures such as satisfaction surveys belong in the same review. The outcome-first school, closest to modern OKR practice, signs that the goal and its target are primary and the instrument is whatever is available, surveys and manual audits included; it will not sign the behaviourist restriction, which it says silently narrows ambition to what the SDK already emits. The single-number school signs that an organisation can hold only one metric in its head and that GAME's job is to find it; it will not sign that a portfolio of five is manageable. The sceptics — Goodhart's law as restated by Marilyn Strathern in 1997, Donald Campbell's 1976 law on corrupted social indicators, Jerry Muller's The Tyranny of Metrics — sign that any metric given a target degrades as a measure; they will not sign that better derivation solves it, since the corruption comes from the target, not the derivation.

Mechanics in depth: what expert practitioners actually compute

The step usually left implicit is the one Rukmini's two teams were arguing about without naming it: choosing an Action is a classification problem. Let G be the event that the user attains the goal over some horizon and A the candidate action observed in an early window. Three quantities govern the choice. Lift, P(G | A) against P(G | not A), is how sharply the action discriminates. Coverage, or recall, P(A | G), is the share of eventual goal-attainers who performed it — an action can discriminate beautifully and describe almost nobody. Incidence, P(A), is how much of the population is eligible to be moved at all. Tulja Fresh's November 2025 cohort of 42,000 new buyers, with the goal operationalised as three or more orders in the month ending day 90 — a base rate of 24% — produced the table below.

Read the table the way an expert does. The app-opens row is the classic vanity action: it covers 59% of successful users but barely discriminates, because it measures presence rather than progress. The slot-preference row is worse — a 1.2× lift is noise dressed as insight. The genuine contest is between the second-order row, which combines strong lift with 70% coverage, and the saved-basket row, whose 63% conditional probability is the highest on the board but which describes only 12% of buyers and captures under a third of eventual successes. Rukmini's data-science lead was reading down the P(G|A) column; her growth lead was reading the lift-times-coverage product. Both were right about their own column.

Figure 2. Tulja Fresh's five candidate actions plotted on lift against coverage. Only the upper-right quadrant supports a company-level activation target; the saved-basket action is a strong signal about a small population, which makes it a segmentation tool rather than a north star.

The effect that decides the argument is causal, not statistical. A high P(G|A) may mean the action produces progress, or merely that users already destined to succeed happen to perform it. Saved baskets illustrate the latter risk: the household that builds a standing list in week one was going to order weekly regardless. An expert therefore does not promote an action on correlation alone; they run a cheap intervention that moves P(A) and ask whether P(G) moves with it. Tulja Fresh's March holdout pushed a basket-save prompt to a random 50% of new buyers. Basket-saving rose from 12% to 29%; ninety-day survival in the treated arm rose from 24.1% to 24.9%, inside the noise band. The correlation was real and the causal content close to nil.

That test has a price, and it is the step most teams skip. Detecting a three-percentage-point absolute change on a 24% base with 80% power at the 5% level requires roughly 16 × p(1−p) ÷ δ², or 16 × 0.1824 ÷ 0.0009 ≈ 3,240 users per arm — a day and a half of Tulja Fresh's acquisition. Sankalan, detecting a ten-point change on an 80% renewal base, would need about 16 × 0.16 ÷ 0.01 ≈ 256 accounts per arm against a population of 140. Its Evaluate step therefore cannot be statistical at all, and pretending otherwise is the characteristic enterprise failure.

What Devdatta did instead is the legitimate small-n practice. He ran the chain separately for each goal-holder — nursing staff who want to leave a shift without paperwork waiting, the medical-records officer who wants clean documentation for insurance claims, the CFO who wants fewer rejected claims — and then looked for an action held by the people who use the product daily rather than those who sign the contract. He settled on discharge summary completed in the application within two hours of the discharge order. Across 53 accounts decided in the prior year, of the 36 accounts scoring above 55% on that measure, 34 renewed; of the 17 scoring below 30%, only 9 did. He could not compute a confidence interval worth quoting, but he could read all seventeen accounts by hand — a form of evidence the consumer team does not have and consistently undervalues.

When the framework applies, and when it misleads

Three conditions make GAME load-bearing, each testable. First, the goal must be attainable within an observable horizon. Tulja Fresh passes: a grocery habit reveals itself within ninety days. Sankalan passes weakly — the CFO's goal of fewer rejected claims resolves over two quarters of billing cycles, so the chain must anchor on the nurse's faster-resolving goal and treat the CFO's as lagging confirmation. Second, the action must be observable without changing the behaviour being observed; both pass, though two Sankalan sites restrict telemetry on data-residency grounds. Third, the population must be large enough, or legible enough, that movement can be distinguished from noise. Rukmini passes on volume; Devdatta only by substituting case-by-case legibility for statistics.

GAME is actively misleading in three situations. It misleads when the product's value is concentrated in a rare, high-stakes event — an insurance claim, a hospital emergency, a fraud block — because the goal-attainment rate is so low that no early action can be validated against it in any useful window, and teams end up measuring rehearsal instead of performance. It misleads when the user's goal is explicitly to use the product less: a debt-repayment app, a screen-time controller, a device-monitoring tool whose ideal state is silence. And it misleads in the first months of a genuinely new category, where the team does not yet know what the goal is; running GAME there produces a chain with the syntax of rigour and the content of a guess, which is more dangerous than an openly provisional number.

Hard edge cases and what happens at the seams

In multi-product companies the chain breaks at the account boundary. Sankalan's documentation and scheduling modules have different goal-holders inside the same hospital, so an account-level composite averages a delighted nursing floor with an indifferent theatre roster and produces a number true of nobody. Mature practice keeps chains per product and per persona, reserving the account roll-up for commercial forecasting, never for product decisions.

In two-sided markets the chain must be run twice and read against itself, because the sides are coupled: a change that raises one side's action rate at the other's expense looks like success for two quarters and reverses in the third, once supply erodes. The worked numbers appear below.

Regulated products constrain the Action step directly. In Indian consumer lending, the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending framework and the fair-practices code make certain behaviours unavailable as activation actions: a chain treating took a second loan as evidence of I want to be financially stable is not a weak proxy but a suitability problem, because optimising it drives the firm toward lending to people the goal itself says should borrow less. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 adds purpose limitation — instrumentation must have been collected for a declared purpose, so mining any available log for candidate actions is not lawfully open.

Hardware plus software introduces two structural gaps: part of the action happens off-device and is never logged, and the release cadence that would let you act on the metric is quarterly. AI-native products fail more subtly: the convenient action, acceptance of a model suggestion, is contaminated by the model itself. At Srot AI, a contract-review assistant sold to Indian legal teams, acceptance ran at 62% but only 38% of accepted suggestions survived into the signed document; a model upgrade then lifted acceptance to 71% with no change in surviving edits. The activation metric had moved without any goal being better served. In AI products the action must be measured downstream of the output — what the human kept — not at the point of interaction.

At the organisational seams the honest account differs from the official one. Mature companies say they derive metrics bottom-up from user goals. What usually happens is that finance fixes a growth number in the annual plan, product constructs a chain terminating conveniently at that number, and the goal sentence is written last, backwards from the metric. The tell is chronology: ask when the interviews behind the goal statement were conducted; if they came after the metric was named, the chain is a justification, not a derivation. Firms that handle this well institutionalise the sequence — a quarterly re-derivation in which goal sentences are rewritten from that quarter's research before anyone looks at the existing dashboard.

Nine nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. Coverage failure hides inside a beautiful conditional probability

The tell is a metric with a spectacular conversion rate and a tiny denominator, defended on the rate alone. The obvious reading — strongest predictor, so make it the target — is wrong, because a target on a low-coverage action instructs the organisation to spend its effort on the 12% who already behave that way, leaving the other 68% of eventual successes unmanaged.

2. Correlation-selected actions decay the moment they are incentivised

The tell is a relationship that was strong in a passive period and weakens after a nudge campaign. The obvious reading is that the campaign was poorly executed; the correct reading is that the action was a marker of user type, and forcing it on a different type severed the link it was selected for. The predictive power belonged to the users, not the behaviour.

3. The goal sentence must survive being read back to a real user

The tell is a goal containing a product noun — "use the repeat-basket feature regularly." Real users state goals in terms of their week, not the product's object model. This looks like a stylistic quibble and is not: a goal naming a feature can only generate actions inside that feature, which is how GAME chains become instruments for defending existing roadmaps.

4. Window length is a design decision, not a default

The tell is a fourteen-day activation window chosen because the analytics tool defaults to it. The window should come from the natural period of the behaviour — a grocery habit cycles weekly, a discharge daily, a renewal annually. Shorter than that period, the window measures reachability; longer, it dilutes the signal with users who would have succeeded anyway.

5. The denominator is where most disputes actually live

Two teams reporting different numbers for the same metric are almost always disagreeing about who is in the population, not what is counted. The expert states the denominator aloud before the numerator — new buyers acquired in a calendar month, excluding coupon-sourced and internal accounts — because an unstated denominator is where cohort definitions drift quarter over quarter and make a trend line meaningless.

6. Guardrail metrics are part of the chain, not an afterthought

Every action promoted to a target should arrive with the counter-metric that would reveal it being gamed. Guardrails look like a compliance formality; in fact the guardrail encodes the team's own theory of how it would cheat under pressure, and a team that cannot name that mechanism has not thought hard enough about its incentives.

7. A metric that cannot move fast enough to be reviewed is the wrong metric for that cadence

The tell is a weekly review in which a number has not moved outside its noise band for eleven straight weeks. The usual conclusion is that nothing is working; the correct one is that cadence and the metric's natural period are mismatched, and the weekly forum needs an input metric while the quarterly forum keeps the output one.

8. Segmentation before aggregation, always

A flat aggregate is the commonest disguise for two populations moving in opposite directions. The expert's reflex on a stubbornly flat line is not to hunt for interventions but to cut the population by the goal users are pursuing, because the intervention that helps one cluster often harms the other and the aggregate is the two effects cancelling.

9. The Evaluate step must name a decision, not a discussion

The tell is the phrase "we'll keep an eye on it." A metric whose only consequence is attention is not managed. The expert insists on a written trigger with a threshold and a named consequence — pause acquisition spend, escalate, open a discovery sprint — because the decision is what makes the number's precision worth paying for. If no decision changes at any value, stop collecting it.

How the practice differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the constraint is causality, not sample size: actions are abundant and correlationally rich, so the discipline is resisting the plausible chain experiments do not support. In B2B and enterprise the constraint inverts — sample sizes preclude inference, goal-holders multiply, and the buyer's goal diverges from the user's. In platform and marketplace businesses the essential addition is the cross-side counter-metric; in hardware, an explicit statement of telemetry coverage and its bias; in AI, a downstream retention-of-output measure, because interaction-level acceptance moves with the model.

By stage the difference is real but narrower than usually claimed. Seed-stage teams should run GAME qualitatively and refuse to set targets, since a target on an unvalidated action hard-codes a guess. Growth-stage companies gain most, having enough users for inference and few enough people for the chain to stay legible. Late-stage companies find derivation easy and Evaluate politically hard, because a dozen teams have a stake in the number. What is not different by stage is the Goal step: both ends of the range need a sentence a real user would recognise, and both are equally tempted to skip writing it.

Three worked examples, including one that failed

Sanchari Mobility — the two-sided chain read against itself

Sanchari Mobility, an intercity cab marketplace between Pune, Nashik and Kolhapur, wrote two goals: the rider's "I want to be sure a car will turn up" and the driver's "I want a day where most of my logged-in hours are paid." The rider action was a completed trip with no reassignment; the driver action, a paid-engaged hour. In July 2025 the team widened the broadcast radius to speed assignment. Rider fill rose from 89% to 94% in three weeks. On the driver side, paid-engaged share fell from 61% to 52% as more drivers chased each request and lost, and driver thirty-day retention fell from 74% to 63%. By week eleven the supply loss had pushed rider fill to 87%, below where it started. Each chain was correct; the aggregate was wrong because the sides were coupled. The fix was to make driver paid-engaged share an explicit guardrail on any rider-side target.

Udyan Devices — the coverage problem in hardware

Udyan Devices sells water sub-metering to housing societies. The facility manager's goal — "I want to stop arguing about bills" — produced the action a disputed reading resolved in the app without a site visit and the metric of disputes per 1,000 billed connections per month, which fell from 14.2 to 5.6 over three quarters. But gateway telemetry reached only 71% of the installed base, and the missing 29% were disproportionately older buildings with weaker connectivity and, on manual audit of 40 such societies, a dispute rate near 11 per 1,000 — making the true figure closer to 7.2. Udyan now publishes the coverage percentage beside every metric and audits a stratified sample of the dark installations quarterly, matching review cadence to the firmware release cadence rather than the sprint.

Sahasra Lending — the chain that broke when it was given a target

Sahasra Lending, a small-ticket personal-loan business, found that borrowers completing full income verification within 48 hours repaid materially better; across 2024 cohorts the rank correlation between branch-level completion share and 24-month repayment was 0.68. The team set a target and added a ₹ 100 cashback and a three-message nudge sequence. Completion rose from 31% to 58% in two quarters — and the correlation with repayment fell to 0.41, while 90-plus-day delinquency on incentivised cohorts rose from 3.2% to 4.9%. The action had been a signal of conscientiousness; paying for it recruited the behaviour without the trait. Recovery took three quarters. The team split the metric into unprompted and incentivised completion, and found the unprompted version retained a 0.61 correlation while the incentivised version carried almost none; then wrote a standing rule that an action may be reported without a target while under validation and acquires one only after an experiment shows that moving it moves the goal. Learning this late cost roughly ₹ 4.1 crore of incremental provisioning.

Failure modes, their early warning signs and the cost of lateness

Proxy decay under incentive. Early sign: the action's rate rises faster than the goal rate. Diagnostic: has the correlation between action and goal attainment been recomputed since the target was set? Caught late, as at Sahasra, the cost is credit or churn losses already booked.

Instrumentation-led action selection. Early sign: every action maps to an event the SDK emitted by default. Diagnostic: which action required new instrumentation? A chain that required none was almost certainly reverse-engineered from the log schema.

Denominator drift. Early sign: a metric improves in a period with no shipped change. Diagnostic: is today's cohort definition identical to the one used when the target was set? Late, the cost is a year of trend data that cannot be compared with itself.

Single-holder capture. Early sign: the goal sentence uses the buyer's vocabulary, not the daily user's. Diagnostic: whose calendar does this goal live in? Caught late, it shows up as healthy usage numbers on accounts that churn without warning.

Telemetry blindness. Early sign: nobody can state the metric's coverage as a percentage. Diagnostic: what fraction of the eligible population could physically produce this event, and how does the excluded fraction differ? Late, the cost is a confident number wrong in a known direction.

Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether the Goal must belong to the user. Purists argue that business objectives in the Goal slot produce metrics optimising the firm's convenience and eventually harming the user, citing engagement-maximising feeds. The business-goal camp answers that user goals are inferred, unverifiable and endlessly re-writable, giving a team infinite latitude to explain away bad numbers, whereas gross margin cannot be re-written in a workshop. The purists would be wrong if firms anchoring on user goals systematically under-performed commercially; the business camp would be wrong if user-goal-anchored chains reliably produced better long-run retention, which the evidence suggests but does not settle.

Whether an action needs causal validation before it gets a target. Experimentalists hold that any unvalidated action is a Sahasra waiting to happen. The velocity camp answers that most startups will not survive long enough to run the test, that correlational activation targets have demonstrably helped many companies, and that a wrong target usually costs a quarter, not a company. The experimentalist position weakens in low-volume products where the test is infeasible; the velocity position weakens wherever the metric touches money, credit or safety.

One number or a portfolio. The single-metric camp rests on attention: a firm can align a thousand people behind one number and cannot behind six. The portfolio camp rests on the fact that every single metric is gameable and that a small set with explicit counter-metrics is the only stable configuration. Neither has evidence strong enough to close the question; the right answer probably depends on how much the organisation's incentives already reward gaming.

Research-derived goals or behaviourally clustered ones. The research-first school says clustering only finds patterns in what the product already permits and can never discover an unserved goal. The data-first school says interview-derived goals reflect what users can articulate, under-representing habitual and low-salience behaviour. Each names a real blind spot in the other, and the field has not settled which costs more.

What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied GAME produces a tidy four-row table and defends it. Someone who has internalised it differs in four observable ways. They state the denominator before the numerator. They treat every proposed action as a hypothesis with a lift, a coverage and a pending causal test, and say aloud which of the three is not yet measured. They write the guardrail in the same sitting as the target, because they can articulate how they themselves would cheat. And they re-derive the chain on a schedule from fresh research rather than defending last year's — because a GAME chain is a claim about a population's behaviour, and populations change while dashboards do not.

What the two protagonists decided

Rukmini chose the second-order action as Tulja Fresh's activation metric at a target of 44% of new buyers, owned by the growth director, reviewed weekly, with a written trigger: below 38% for three consecutive weeks, new-city launches pause. She kept the saved-basket action but demoted it to a reported, untargeted segmentation signal, citing the March holdout that showed its predictive power was not causal. Her reasoning: coverage, not conditional probability, determines how much of the business a target can govern.

Devdatta adopted the two-hour discharge-completion measure as Sankalan's leading renewal indicator at a threshold of 55%, owned jointly by the customer-success and product leads, reviewed monthly per account rather than weekly in aggregate, with a named consequence: any account below 30% for two consecutive months triggers an on-site discovery visit within three weeks. He declined to quote a confidence interval, telling the board that with 140 accounts the company would manage by reading cases, not estimating parameters — a statement of method they found more reassuring than a spurious statistic.

Three questions for discussion. First, had Tulja Fresh's holdout shown a two-point rather than a 0.8-point lift on ninety-day survival, would that justify promoting the saved-basket action at 32% coverage — and what is the exchange rate between lift and coverage? Second, Sankalan anchors on the nurse's goal while the renewal is signed by a CFO whose goal resolves two quarters later; when does anchoring on the daily user become an expensive mistake? Third, Sahasra split one metric into prompted and unprompted variants — durable solution, or has the Goodhart problem simply moved one step upstream to await the next incentive?
